speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This Bill proposes amendments to the Administration of Muslim Law Act 1966, or AMLA.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Before we go into the specific amendments of this Bill, I would like to first briefly share with Members the context of the AMLA and how it supports our Muslim community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The AMLA was enacted shortly after our Independence to cover key aspects of Muslim life in Singapore, so that the personal matters of Muslims such as marriage, divorce and their estates could continue to be governed by Muslim law.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Singapore is one of a handful of countries that have such laws specifically for a minority Muslim community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is under the AMLA that the Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura, or MUIS, was established as a statutory board to administer the religious affairs of the Singapore Muslim community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The AMLA provides for a Mufti to be appointed and for religious decisions issued by him to be recognised.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Other statutory Muslim institutions such as the Syariah Court, or SYC, and the Registry of Muslim Marriages, or ROMM, were also constituted under the AMLA.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The AMLA has been reviewed regularly to ensure that this set of laws remain relevant to the community’s socio-religious needs because we live in a fast-changing and complex environment.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For this round of AMLA amendments, we seek to update the provisions governing the processes and operations of our statutory Muslim institutions, namely MUIS, SYC and ROMM.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) published a draft of this Bill for public consultations late last year.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We appreciate the broad support from the community for this Bill and the valuable feedback received.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: However, the wakaf that were created in the past are no longer sufficient nor flexible enough to meet the evolving needs of the Muslim community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We need to create and steward sustainable financial resources to support the community's long-term social and religious development.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will require us to rejuvenate our wakaf spirit to enable more members of the community to contribute.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In this regard, I initiated a plan to establish the Wakaf Masyarakat Singapura, or WMS.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The WMS will enable more individuals to bequeath their assets for future generations and for our Muslim community to remain financially self-reliant and capable to address future needs and challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I am heartened by the support and encouraging feedback from the community for this initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This amendment Bill will empower MUIS to create wakaf and serve as the overarching legal foundation for the WMS.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The WMS will generate a more sustainable revenue stream to fund the broader and evolving socio-religious needs of the community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These needs include the renewal of mosque leases and mosque maintenance, the development of religious teachers and scholars, collectively known as asatizah, and other community programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Individuals can contribute voluntarily to the WMS in the form of cash, property or Central Provident Fund (CPF) nominations.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over time, as proceeds are sustained, the WMS will complement established community funds, such as the Mosque Building and MENDAKI Fund, or MBMF, and zakat.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This amendment Bill will also strengthen MUIS' ability to manage the MBMF by clarifying that any contribution to the MBMF that is not attributable to any individual is deemed to be for the purpose of mosque building, so as to benefit all members of the Singapore Muslim community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MUIS will enhance its recognition framework for Foreign Halal Certification Bodies, or FHCB, as part of its efforts to provide a transparent, practical and high-quality system of halal certification.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These FHCBs, which are based in exporting countries, certify food products that are produced or manufactured overseas for import to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This amendment Bill will strengthen the administration of the FHCB scheme by setting out the legal framework for the recognition of these bodies as having comparable halal certification benchmarks to MUIS' Halal Certification Standards.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will provide greater transparency and assurance to our Muslim community on the quality of MUIS-recognised FHCBs and provide our Muslim consumers and businesses with greater assurance when purchasing and consuming halal food products.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As provided for under the AMLA, MUIS' Legal Committee, also known as the Fatwa Committee, issues fatwas, or religious rulings, which help guide the community in navigating socio-religious issues.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will allow the Committee to tap on a wider range of expertise, such as within the asatizah fraternity.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Fatwa Committee will also be empowered to decide on whether there is a need to issue a fatwa based on the requests received.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For example, there is no need to issue a fatwa if the Office of the Mufti has already issued religious guidance or an advisory known as irsyad on a specific issue.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Fatwa deliberations can therefore be focused on issues that have an important bearing on the life of our Muslim community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will help to prioritise the Committee's efforts and resources.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MUIS' Fatwa Committee has had to formulate guidance on new, special and unique issues facing the Malay/Muslim community here over the decades.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The strong and decisive leadership of the Fatwa Committee has guided our community well and more broadly supported Singapore, through the COVID-19 pandemic and beyond.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For their religious leadership during the pandemic, our Mufti Dr Nazirudin Nasir and the Fatwa Committee were conferred the Imam Al-Qarafi Award by the General Secretariat for Fatwa Authorities under the prestigious Dar al-Ifta, one of the world's pre-eminent Islamic institutions.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This recognition is testament to the quality of our Muslim religious leaders and their religious guidance.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: More importantly, it reflects the trust and confidence that our Singapore Muslim community places in these religious leaders.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will preserve and strengthen the high levels of trust and confidence in our religious teachers and religious education and continue to enhance MUIS' administration of Muslim religious schools.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These provisions will augment MUIS' ability to administer all Muslim religious schools in Singapore, on both online and physical platforms and enable MUIS to take enforcement action against any unregistered Muslim religious school here.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will ensure that Islamic religious education in Singapore is conducted by accredited institutions and asatizah with the necessary qualifications.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will maintain the integrity of our religious sector in guiding our Muslim community on the practice of Islam in a modern and multi-religious society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Recent digitalisation efforts by the ROMM and the SYC will enable them to better serve and support Muslim families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Similar to the case for civil marriages, this digital Certificate will not require the signatures of the Muslim marriage solemniser, also known as the Kadi or Naib Kadi, the marrying parties and their witnesses.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This amendment Bill will also facilitate the implementation of SYC's new digital case management system.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We will remove the requirements for the divorce register to be signed by the Registrar of SYC and the witnesses whose evidence has been taken by the Court, for cases where a married woman has applied for a divorce on the ground of fasakh under section 49 of the AMLA, that is, judicial dissolution of marriage based on Muslim law as provided by the AMLA.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These amendments will not change the fact that Muslim law will continue to apply to Muslim marriages and divorces.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The requirements of a valid Muslim marriage and divorce must and will be ensured even with these amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The digitalisation of Muslim marriage and divorce services will be carried out in full respect of the solemnity and significance of the occasion, while enhancing convenience for the community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The amendments align SYC's processes and powers with that of the Family Justice Courts, which were amended last year.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This amendment Bill will enhance SYC's powers to deliver fair and just outcomes through the judge-led approach in its administration of divorces for Muslim families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This includes allowing SYC to make orders on its own motion, including an order of a substantive nature to better facilitate the just, expeditious and economical resolution or disposal of any matter.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will ensure that SYC has the powers to address the immediate needs of the family.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Currently, SYC can only make a substantive order if it is pleaded or applied for by the parties.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This amendment Bill will also allow SYC to limit a party from filing an application or a document in support of an application in certain situations.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Such applications include those that are or are likely to be without merit, based on the applicant's past conduct, or where the application or document will have an adverse effect on the welfare of a minor child, who is an individual below 21 years in age.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will prevent parties from filing applications that may result in prolonged proceedings, unnecessary acrimony and hardship on others involved.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Amendments will also be made to sections 35 and 52 of the AMLA to clarify SYC's jurisdiction and powers in respect of ancillary orders, such as the custody, care and control and access of minor children upon divorce or nullification of marriage.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: WMS is a form of giving recurring charity for the benefit of the next generation, which is a practice often carried out in Islam and was a norm for our ancestors.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The setting up of the WMS seeks to rejuvenate this wakaf spirit in the community, after the last wakaf made by Shaikh Taha Abubakar Mattar for the land where Masjid Sallim Mattar sits in 1978.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: A community wakaf that we create together, for the benefit of the whole community, especially for future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This will be done by setting out the legal framework for the recognition of Foreign Halal Certification Bodies (FHCB) that have certification standards that are comparable to MUIS'.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is to ensure that all Muslim religious schools in Singapore, both online and physical, are properly certified.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Fourth, to strengthen the Fatwa (Legal) Committee by expanding the Committee's membership and allowing for greater discretion in considering requests for fatwas.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Fatwa Committee's efforts and resources will also be focused on fatwa requests that have a significant impact on our Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It also includes amendments to digitalise ROMM and Syariah Court processes, in addition to enhancing provisions to administer these two entities for a more effective outcome.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the Bill covers several important aspects, allow me to focus on two key areas, firstly, providing MUIS with powers to create wakafs, and secondly, the recognition of Foreign Halal Certification Bodies.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On empowering MUIS to create wakafs, as shared by the Minister, community funds such as zakat as well as donations to mosques and madrasahs and the Mosque Building and MENDAKI Fund, only supports the day-to-day and short-term needs of the Muslim community, including the cost of operating 72 mosques in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must also prepare for the needs of our Muslim community in the medium and long term.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This includes making sure that our madrasahs are well funded in a sustainable manner, so that we can continue to provide quality education.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Besides providing a good grounding in Islamic education, we must provide multiple development pathways for our asatizah.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will help us nurture future religious leaders who can continue to provide guidance to our community in an increasingly complex global environment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An example is the Wakaf Masyarakat Singapura whose donors comprise members of the Muslim community in Singapore, rather than an individual or a family.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This means that everyone in the Muslim community can contribute, regardless of the size of contribution, towards the future needs of the community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to seek a clarification.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While clauses 15 to 18 explain what the wakafs can be used for, and how it can be administered, this Bill does not mention any restriction on donors to the wakafs created by MUIS.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can these wakafs accept contribution from foreign donors?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And if so, how do we prevent foreign actors from influencing the intent and direction of the created wakafs to support the medium and long-term needs of the Muslim community in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore relies heavily on imported food products to meet local demand.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From this perspective, it is important for any food seller or food establishments possessing MUIS halal certification to have access to a wide range of halal product supplies that meet MUIS' halal certification standards.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of such food companies or establishments import products that bear the halal certification logo given by Foreign Halal Certification Bodies (FHCBs).

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What will be the prerequisites for a Foreign Halal Certification Body to be recognized by MUIS?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will MUIS impose requirements for regular audits to these FHCBs so that their food products continue to be certified as halal in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If so, how do we prevent this process from being excessively burdensome for MUIS, since this Bill will not involve additional expenditures?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will the proposed legal framework strengthen MUIS' jurisdiction over the FHCBs and ensure that the FHCBs meet MUIS' halal certification standards?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will the standards imposed by MUIS on FHCBs help our halal-certified business and Muslim consumers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, the amendment to the AMLA is substantive, comprehensive and reflects the needs of the community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It shows that continuous renewal efforts are needed as we live in today's fast-paced world.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Once again, Sir, I would like to reiterate the Workers' Party's support towards the changes, improvements and enhancements that will be made.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, I have several questions that aim to seek clarifications on several clauses that will be introduced or amended so that the Muslim community in Singapore can better understand why the proposed amendments in the Bill are needed, as well as the benefits and gains that it will bring.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My question to the Minister with regards to this matter is, firstly, whether the Minister can give some elaboration on the existing recognition process, such as what the current weaknesses are; and also, what are the main reasons that prompted MUIS to embark on these reforms.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I understand that these laws were made to tighten regulations over the teaching of Islam and also to empower MUIS to conduct inspections and monitoring, and also take certain actions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: All these are aimed at preventing any deviant teachings.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And perhaps it may be useful for the Minister to clarify whether these 10 individuals also comprise a cumulative figure rather than just a class attended by 10 individuals at any one time.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I think this clarification is important because an individual who wants to spread deviant teachings will just simply break up their sessions into nine individuals at any one time.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to seek clarification on the following situations, that is, whether they are subject to the definition of Muslim religious school'.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second, what about zikir and maulid sessions which are often held at a house and attended by 10 or more individuals?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Will such situations also fall under this category?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Moving on, Sir, I would like to touch on the expansion of the Fatwa Committee membership as well as granting more discretion to the Committee in considering requests to issue a fatwa.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I would like a clarification from the Minister on how the process of filling up this new position will be carried out.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For example, does the selection of Committee members require one to make an application or will it be done only through the selection and nomination process by MUIS?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Also, can the Minister explain, what are the limitations of existing laws that requires an amendment to be made to section 32, where subsection (3) is replaced with a new subsection (3A)?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: My questions are as follows, one, what is the estimated yearly amount that will channeled; and two, how long has this been going on, and why was this change or amendment not done much earlier?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The enhancement of operations and expansion of powers will be much needed to enable these two bodies to provide effective and efficient services that keeps pace with the rapid development of society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: With expanded powers and enhanced operations, it is hoped that these two institutions will be supported with the necessary resources, especially manpower resources, so that they can achieve the objectives set for them as best as possible.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill reflects our dedication to the evolving needs of our Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Specifically, I wish to address the definition and administration of Muslim religious schools under the auspices of the MUIS, and how this impacts our community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As we evolve as a society, our laws and regulations must also adapt to new challenges and opportunities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   I think we can all agree that in such egregious cases, there needs to be a balance struck somewhere, to allow offenders to have a second chance while also keeping the vulnerable protected.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I would also like to echo feedback that I have received from lawyers who regularly handled such cases, that we would need more clarity on how the assessment will be conducted and what are the criteria for an unconditional discharge.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I also hope that to be fair to offenders, there can be additional and dedicated resources provided to support offenders convicted under SEPP in their rehabilitation journey in prison.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The Administration of Muslim Law Act (AMLA), enacted in 1968, outlines the establishment and functions of key Islamic institutions in Singapore, including Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS), the Syariah Court and the Registry of Muslim Marriages (ROMM).

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The Act also covers the administration of mosques, as well as the creation and distribution of wakafs, or Islamic charitable endowments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Since 1968, this Act has been amended several times, most recently in February 2022 when provisions governing the operation of statutory Muslim institutions were modernised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Maintaining this balance respects Muslims as individuals and Islam as a faith, and enhances the well-being of both the Muslim community and Singapore society as a whole.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, before I do so, I would like to note that I am Vice-President of Persatuan Pemudi Islam Singapura, or the Singapore Muslim Women’s Association.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By directing wakaf funds strategically, we can address pressing needs in education, healthcare and social services, thereby benefiting both donors and beneficiaries and enhancing the overall well-being of the Muslim community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The proposal is also aligned with the Forward SG strategy, which focuses on collective responsibility and developing a kind, compassionate and caring society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Enhancing and supporting wakaf, and providing opportunities to contribute to the community, both empower Muslims and allow them to act consistently with their faith.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Wakaf is an Arabic term meaning "to stop, contain or to preserve", and, traditionally, the returns from the wakaf structure are disbursed according to the wishes of the individual or family making the donation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: These wakaf funds will be held collectively by MUIS, and the returns are then distributed by MUIS according to perceived community need, thereby making disbursements according to the wishes of the donor difficult.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This targeted approach would also facilitate easier access to funds for entities, such as mosques or social service agencies, and would preserve the traditional and religious objectives of wakaf, and also remain responsive to evolving cultural and social dynamics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike zakat, which is a requirement for all Muslims, wakaf is not compulsory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, the frequency and level of wakaf donations will fluctuate over time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While this amendment offers Muslim consumers more choices and stimulates competition, there is currently no prohibition on the import and sale of products from halal certification bodies not recognised by MUIS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As this may result in confusion among consumers, perhaps it might be helpful for MUIS to undertake a community education campaign informing consumers about the FHCBs recognised by MUIS and those that are not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This would allow consumers to make informed choices over the halal products they purchase that are consistent with their dietary and religious preference and obligations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It may also be helpful for MUIS to develop an app, similar to MuslimSG, to assist consumers to identify FHCBs recognised by MUIS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The proposal to expand the Legal Committee to allow for better representation of the Asatizah fraternity will enhance the expertise of the Committee and, therefore, the capacity of the Committee to decide and respond to queries and provide informed fatwa rulings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I do, however, have some comments about this matter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: With their targeted programming and engagement, the needs of the Muslim community are met.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While the majority are Sunni Muslims of Malay heritage, most of whom follow the Shafi'i or Hanafi school of thoughts, there are also Muslims with Indian heritage, as well as converts and migrants from various parts of the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This diversity is testament to Singapore's acceptance of all faiths and adds significantly to the rich socio-religious fabric of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It also supports the need to expand the Legal Committee, so as to reflect and respond to an evolving community of Muslims facing ever-changing questions about Islamic practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by the Singapore Mufti, Ustaz Dr Nazirudin Mohd Nasir, at the appointment of the most recent Fatwa Committee, and I quote: "…in providing guidance for current and future issues, there should be a fresh application of Islamic traditions to contemporary issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The Committee should also deliberate on moral and ethical considerations and look at longer-term implications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This approach will further empower the Committee to produce innovative, progressive and contextualised fatwas for the Muslim community to lead their religious lives confidently".

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, the proposed expansion is a positive step and will ensure that the Legal Committee authentically mirrors the richness and diversity of Singapore's Muslim population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As we continue with this expansion, I seek clarification about steps taken to ensure the continued selection of qualified Asatizahs with the expertise and knowledge needed to address all issues raised by the Muslim community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Related, I also seek clarification about how the Committee actively seeks and encourages submissions and feedback from all members of Singapore's diverse Muslim community and how these submissions are responded to in a timely and respectful manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is important that the Committee is accessible to the Muslim and broader community, and that community members have confidence that their submissions will be received, considered and responded to in a timely, transparent and equitable manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For children especially, the school environment should be one that makes them comfortable and safe, and, while at school, they should be taught a standardised, relevant and approved curriculum and not be exposed to any form of abuse or harm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: And just like all other schools, teachers within Muslim religious schools need to be people who are safe to work with children and adults, and are suitably qualified to teach their subject area.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By developing a common definition of Muslim religious schools, we are able to strengthen the trust of individuals, parents and the broader community, so that they are clear about the approval process, what is being taught, how it is being taught and who is doing the teaching.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I do, however, seek clarification about the policies and procedures MUIS and/or the Ministry have to ensure that all Muslim religious schools meet all required accountability and quality standards and, in addition, what those standards are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, I seek clarification about the content in the training framework that covers contemporary issues facing the Muslim community and the best way to respond to these issues in a sensitive manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, I seek clarification about the content in the training framework that covers working with children in an age-appropriate manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This, however, is sometimes difficult when considered against personal definitions of inappropriate or extreme; differences of opinion within Islam about what is correct, and the right of people to share personal views with friends or family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, I seek clarification about how the proposed amendments manage this balance, particularly with respect to at-home, private, religious education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The advent of digitalisation promises convenience and efficiency in managing marriage and divorce procedures, and online accessibility to documents can simplify the process, making it more user-friendly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Some clients of Syariah Court have, however, expressed concerns about difficulties navigating the system, particularly in filing and retrieving online documents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Accordingly, I seek clarification about how the proposed digital system address user experience challenges, and ensures a seamless process for all clients?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While the move towards online solemnisation offers flexibility, it also raises important questions about the default mode of solemnisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is an important issue, specifically for selected groups of individuals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: One significant concern is how to prevent verification errors, or, worse, instances of scamming.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For transnational couples, there are also questions about the recognition of digital certificates from countries other than Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is an important issue, given the need to ensure the validity of digital documents across international borders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The introduction of an online divorce system is progressive, and aims to ease the process and support the couple with their application.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The system may also be of particular benefit to individuals experiencing family violence, as it offers a discreet and accessible avenue for seeking legal remedies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is important to address the unique challenges faced by individuals in such situations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: With use of technology, the human aspect is maybe missed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is therefore important that, as we move towards expedient digital processes, there are mechanisms in place to provide additional support for affected individuals, including those impacted by trauma often associated with family violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, there should be an emphasis on educational resources to enhance couples' understanding of the online divorce system, ensuring that victims are empowered with the knowledge needed to navigate the process and make informed decisions about their future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This holistic approach will not only streamline divorce procedures, but also prioritise the well-being and safety of individuals facing family violence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, Syariah Court has commendably prioritised the best-interests of children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This model aims to expedite the exit from conflict zones, enabling individuals to move forward and rebuild their lives with support from community agencies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This is undoubtedly a commendable step, but as we navigate this paradigm shift, we need to be mindful of potential issues faced by the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As we move towards providing support throughout the process, it is equally important to remember after-divorce support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the judge-led model could efficiently connect individuals with relevant community services, ensuring a seamless transition post-divorce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As we embrace these challenges, we strengthen the fabric of Singapore's harmonious society, where each community is valued and empowered to contribute to our shared prosperity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is on the Legal Committee’s process for considering a request and preparing a ruling.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 32(3) requires the Legal Committee to consider every request for a ruling unless the request is frivolous.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 32(3A) provides that the Legal Committee may prepare a ruling on the request if it is appropriate or necessary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the procedure and timelines for the Legal Committee to consider a request and to prepare a ruling?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen resident cases where these rulings are required for Court application.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In one case, the request was submitted in August 2023.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if the Legal Committee are expected to prepare their ruling based on any standards of timeliness?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are there any plans to review the workload of the Legal Committee and the functioning of the Legal Committee to see how such requests can be more effectively managed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the recognition of foreign halal certification bodies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MUIS’ halal certification is well known and trusted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that the halal certification is happening overseas, what special steps will MUIS take to ensure that the standards hold up to local halal certification standards?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third clarification is on the oversight of Muslim religious schools.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 86A inserts a definition of "Muslim religious school".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Majlis are empowered to set rules on these schools, including on how they provide Islamic instruction "online or remotely through electronic means." The Majlis may also make rules for the oversight of Muslim religious schools including the powers to inspect, to obtain information, to gain access to any computer or online account, and to examine any record.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In a situation where Islamic instruction is provided in virtual meeting rooms and the virtual meeting room is hosted on a remote server outside of Singapore, can Minister clarify how these oversight and inspection provisions will apply?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding these clarifications, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In delivering my comments for this Bill, especially in the context of the proposed amendments relating to wakaf, I wish to declare that I am President of Lembaga Biasiswa Kenangan Maulud, which is an Institution of Public Character, a community organisation and charity that supports education of students in need and those who come from underprivileged communities.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: It gives guidance on the establishment of Islamic institutions and religious schools, and appointment of key religious figures within the community, addresses the administration of Muslim Law through our Syariah Courts and supports the need for Muslims to manage religious matters relating to Zakat, wakaf, Hajj and halal matters – among other things.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I have clarifications relating to three areas of the Bill – wakaf, Meaning of Muslim religious schools and Foreign Halal Certification Body.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned about the accessibility of the wakaf created by the Majlis to community organisations.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Where aligned with the intent and purposes of the wakaf, could community organisations and societies serving for the development of Islamic teachers, mosques, madrasahs and socio-religious programmes and initiatives to uplift the Muslim community and the under-privileged make applications as well for funding available through the wakaf?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This would give assurance to the community that this wakaf contributed by the people would and could be accessible to its intended recipients not only through programmes by the Majlis, but also through community organisations and societies serving the same.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Where the Majlis has the power to remove and appoint trustees and mutawallis relating to wakafs created by others, may I clarify that in the instance where the Wakaf itself is now created by the Majlis and it is now appointed trustee to this wakaf, what is the intended supervisory structure to ensure governance and compliance to the intent of this wakaf, and whether should this be enshrined within AMLA as well?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, in relation to the proposed section 86A, on the meaning of Muslim religious schools, I have a clarification on the definition and meaning of Muslim religious schools.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: The stated definition of Muslim religious schools, taking reference from sections 2 and 86A together, are that such schools could also be defined as a person that habitually teaches Quranic recitation, Quranic literacy, Tajwid, Fardh ‘ain and other religious sciences which include, but are not limited to Aqidah, Tafsir, Fiqh and Hadith.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In many Muslim families, such Islamic instruction, habitually or otherwise, is seen as part of family upbringing and a way in which to imbibe and inculcate values to their young.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Many see it as basic tenet of parental or familial responsibility, and one that does not necessarily need formal instruction nor be certified to do so as is the case in formal Islamic instruction in religious schools.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Often, these cover very basic aspects of religion and the way of life of a Muslim within their families and I also imagine this to be a universal approach in many families practising their respective religious faiths, Muslims or otherwise.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This particular definition of the proposed section that a person could be defined as a Muslim religious school, and be subjected to the rules, powers and controls vested to the Majlis, appears potentially intrusive to the Muslim family unit.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: This definition of Muslim religious schools also may entangle parents, or grandparents as the case may be, who want to reach out to their family members, teach values organic to a Muslim family, including very basic areas of Quran literacy and recitation, or values related to the Islamic creed and practice.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, as a young child, my own ability now to be able to read Arabic script and the Quran was the result of habitual Islamic instruction from my elderly grandmother on a regular basis, and this is something which I would not consider as coming close to a definition of a Muslim religious school requiring regulatory oversight.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Could I clarify the intent of including the word "person" as part of the definition of Muslim religious schools, and whether this definition could be nuanced and clarified further to ensure it is not intrusive to, and inadvertently implicate, well-meaning families –and these could be very large families, more than 10 members – that wish to continue their tradition of teaching basic Islamic values habitually within the household?

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, in relation to the proposed section 88AA, on the Foreign Halal Certification Body, as the market for halal certification continues to grow internationally, so too does the proliferation of FHCBs many of whom take example from the professionalism that MUIS has established over decades in halal certification experience.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, the inclusion of section 88AA into AMLA is timely and important.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nominated Member)
text: If the latter is not covered, my view is that members of the public should also be protected against the use of halal certificates and marks from unrecognised FHCBs and even more so, because they can be misleading and in the first instance, arise from FHCBs that MUIS has not formally endorsed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I firstly declare that I am a lawyer with an active practice in the Syariah Bar.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am also a panel counsel for MUIS.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also acknowledge the comprehensive consultations that have been conducted by the Ministry of Law, not only with the public but also legal practitioners, particularly in the Syariah Court bar including those from the Muslim Law Practice Committee (MLPC) of the Law Society of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is through these engagements and consultations that we further improve not only the access to justice but also bring greater efficiency to the Syariah Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These three aspects will be the focus of my speech.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Certificate of Marriage has been an important symbol that marks a significant milestone in the life journey of a married couple.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the digital Certificate of Marriage for Muslim marriages, the signatures of the Muslim marriage solemniser, the marrying parties and their witnesses are no longer required, given the unique and secure identification through Singpass.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In my Court experience, some couples undergoing divorce may face issues locating their own hard copies of Marriage certificate or there are even instances where one party withholds possession of the certificate from the other.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This digital certificate will help prevent these situations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, ROMM still needs to conduct some due diligence, notwithstanding the digitalised process.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the Kadi and Naib Kadi assess that the couples are ready for marriage?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister please clarify what are the safeguards to ensure that the digital database and the digital Certificate are secure against against any tampering, personal identity theft and breaches of cybersecurity?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For couples who wish to have a physical memento of their marriage, will ROMM continue to provide a hard copy of the Certificate of Marriage to them?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this House, I have previously raised issues on implementing a specific dispute resolution mechanism for wakaf in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be beneficial to bring confidence in the utilisation or adoption of wakaf instruments generally and for the WMS specifically.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Presently, any disputes relating to wakaf or removal of mutawalli goes to the High Court.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the case of Valibhoy vs Valibhoy, the High Court held that the jurisdiction and power to manage a wakaf including the removal of a mutawalli and appointment of trustees of a wakaf lay exclusively within the purview of MUIS.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the facts of that case, the High Court did not exercise its residual inherent jurisdiction and attendant powers of the Court over the wakaf.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, that does not mean that similar disputes may not arise in the future.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This brings a unique opportunity for the Syariah Court to be the forum for any such disputes to be the heard through a dispute resolution framework for wakaf, which may include the concept of mediation or arbitration.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would ensure that the correct expertise will be provided and would also allow for matters relating to religious issues and wakaf to be dealt with sensitively and confidentially.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I have some clarifications on the amendments in relation to wakaf.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For WMS or wakaf created by the Majlis, who would be the mutawalli?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Majlis appoint the mutawalli for the WMS in the Gazette or Rules?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Majlis itself be the trustee of the wakaf?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is important because the new section 58(5A) states that certain obligations do not apply if MUIS is the trustee of the wakaf and no mutawalli has been appointed by MUIS.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would be grateful if Minister can clarify who will be the intended trustee of the WMS – whether it will be Majlis itself or another party.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, I move on to the amendments to the Syariah Court jurisdiction and procedure.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Traditionally, the Family Justice Court hears issues of maintenance of children until the age of 21 even after divorce, and this is established both in practice and caselaw.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And what resources will be provided to the Syariah Court to handle maintenance applications for minor children?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And will these affect pending applications for maintenance currently in the Family Justice Court?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, on the proposed section 36B, which involves applications that will likely have an adverse effect on a child’s welfare impending proceedings, what is the legal test and/or standard for “will or is likely to”?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Further, how will the Syariah Court be better supported and resourced in order to hear such applications expeditiously?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I welcome the amendments to ensure that the Syariah Court has the powers to address the immediate needs of the family in a judge-led approach.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would this also extend to interim orders or injunctions that the Court can order?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The parties had to go to the Family Justice Court and the Civil Courts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Malay, Sir. :   In conclusion, Mr Speaker, the amendments to AMLA are steps in the right direction to provide access to justice in a more equitable and efficient manner.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, it ensures that we have the best platform to support the enactment of a Bill to create the Wakaf Masyarakat Singapura (WMS) so that we can leave a lasting and beneficial legacy for many generations to come.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In particular, I welcome the amendments that will help encourage the spirit of giving within our community through the wakaf.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Wakaf is ingrained in our community's religious tradition and history as initially demonstrated by our pioneer philanthropists in the past.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They have set up various wakafs that continue to benefit our community until today.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These amendments are key in providing us with the necessary legal foundation to ensure that the Wakaf Masyarakat Singapura can be successful and garner support from everyone within the community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As the holy month of Ramadan will be upon us in about a month's time, let us nurture the habit of giving and rekindle the spirit of the wakaf within our community to help those in need through perpetual traditions like the wakaf.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I end my speech with a Malay quatrain: Preparing a tray to serve food; The laden tray feels much heavier; The community wakaf is something good; Bringing benefits in this world and the Hereafter.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This enables our statutory Muslim institutions to meet the evolving needs of our community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I am heartened by the strong support from Members and the community to empower MUIS to establish the Wakaf Masyarakat Singapura (WMS).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim raised several questions about the WMS and how MUIS would manage wakaf.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: All members, whether you are rich or poor, you can do it.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: These can be in the form of cash, property or CPF nominations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The WMS will be supported by collective community contributions and used for collective purposes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is unlike traditional wakaf, which are created by individual Muslims and bequeathed for specific purposes as designated by the contributors.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The WMS will also complement existing wakaf that have been created for specific causes such as education, which Assoc Prof Razwana had suggested.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We want the WMS to build a sizeable corpus, such that its long-term returns can benefit the larger community and be flexible enough to meet the evolving socio-religious needs of our community over time in the future.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Muslim individuals who wish to contribute to specific causes may still set up their own wakaf and enliven this wakaf spirit.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As with all wakaf in Singapore, the WMS will be vested in and administered by MUIS under the AMLA.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To Dr Syed Harun’s question, MUIS will appoint a mutawalli once the WMS has been vested and the corpus has been built.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The mutawalli will then manage the wakaf in accordance with the rules, terms and conditions required by MUIS.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The WMS is a wakaf by the community and for the community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In its first instance, the returns from the WMS will be used to sustain our religious institutions, develop our asatizah fraternity, and empower our Singapore Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Over the next 30 years, many of our mosques and madrasahs will face land lease renewals.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The WMS will enable the community to prepare early for these growing needs by harnessing our collective resources in the here and now, instead of having to find funds to meet very sizeable requirements only when they are due.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The WMS will also support efforts to develop and professionalise our asatizah fraternity and nurture competent religious leaders, who are able to guide the community through challenging and contemporary issues.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will take the cue from the use of our national Reserves to assess when our community can use the reserve fund and when it is critically needed to enable our religious institutions to support the community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will study it further in consultation with MUIS and the MUIS Council, our Malay/Muslim community organisations and the broader public.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I agree with Mr Sharael Taha and Assoc Prof Razwana Begum that MUIS must ensure proper governance of WMS and this is what the Bill will require MUIS to do.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As with other wakaf, the WMS must be audited as a matter of public accountability and its financial statements published in MUIS' annual reports.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, they will be presented to Parliament and we can scrutinise them.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The WMS will be held to stringent standards, with clear rules governing its administration.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will give the community confidence that their contributions will make a real and positive impact.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The wakaf funds are primarily placed in property and low-risk investments that can reap a steady income stream whilst preserving its corpus.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As an Islamic endowment fund, MUIS is guided by the Fatwa Committee and the MUIS Investment Committee to ensure that the investments are permissible and that the wakaf objectives can be met.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: All contributions to a wakaf, including WMS, will have their proceeds distributed in accordance with the wakaf's objectives.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Therefore, the contributors will not be able to alter or direct the intent and direction of the wakaf.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This ensures that wakaf are used for charitable and socio-religious purposes that it was originally intended.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Just like other wakafs, any disputes relating to the management of WMS after a mutawalli has been appointed will be managed through the wakaf dispute resolution framework, comprising mediation and inquiry processes institutionalised by MUIS.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The nature of Islamic religious education and Muslim religious schools have changed dramatically since AMLA was first enacted in 1966.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: In fact, we have more qualified teachers amongst us than we had before, people who went to schools overseas and are graduates of esteemed Islamic universities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Religious education also no longer takes place only in a physical school or setting but has also expanded to online platforms and channels.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The AMLA, therefore, needs to be updated to reflect these changes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We need to ensure that religious teachings communicated through various platforms are appropriate for a contemporary and diverse society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Hence, we must continue to strengthen MUIS' administration of our Muslim religious schools, to preserve the high level of confidence that the community places in them.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Dr Wan Rizal asked how the proposed definition of religious schools will impact Islamic religious education in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum asked how MUIS ensures that Muslim religious schools meet quality standards, and Mr Faisal Manap asked where the 10 comes from and how do we define what makes 10.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: First, Islamic education in Singapore must be delivered by individuals who are certified under MUIS' Asatizah Recognition Scheme, or ARS.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They are under the second level, ARS II.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will ensure that our community has access to proper religious guidance from accredited and qualified religious teachers who possess a good understanding of Islamic values and principles and who are attuned to Singapore's context.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Indeed, we should give opportunities to our qualified religious teachers to be the one guiding us because they are not just qualified, they are accredited and they are well-placed to lead us whether it is in Quran reading or religious guidance and we need not go to other secondary sources, more so those from overseas.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To Mr Faisal Manap's "why 10?", this ensures that our definition of a Muslim religious school is in line with the broad understanding of what a school is defined in other legislative Acts.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We are taking a leaf from other legislation to make sure that we are consistent.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Third, the provisions will encompass both online and in-person instruction.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They apply to individuals and organisations based in Singapore and who are conducting online religious classes for 10 or more individuals also physically present in the country.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To Mr Louis Ng's question, these provisions will cover virtual rooms if the individuals attending the classes are physically present in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Fourth, MUIS ensures that Muslim religious schools offer quality education by conducting periodic audits on these institutions and their teachers, and this is important for our community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: For example, ARS-registered teachers have to complete a Continuous Professional Education programme of a prescribed number of hours, to be in touch with the latest development, to be in touch with one another and also with our senior religious teachers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: They cover modules, such as the Code of Ethics, Contemporary Islamic Thought and Modern and Prophetic Pedagogy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Taken together, the robust ARS-registration system, comprehensive asatizah training and the strong IECP regulatory framework seek to uphold the quality delivery of our religious education which means that, if we do this right, then our understanding of Islam, will be well-guided, moderated and also, always in touch with those who are qualified.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: That said, I would like to urge our Muslim community to exercise due diligence and seek religious instruction from credible sources, and, in particular, refer to our ARS-certified teachers to better guide ourselves and our children on religious matters and education.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It is not intended to regulate the private and personal sharing of religious views and opinions between individuals, friends, family members or colleagues or, as Mr Faisal Manap puts it, zikir sessions, or sessions where you are not imparting religious instructions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, it does not apply to all these.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I would now like to turn to Mr Louis Ng's question about fatwas or religious rulings which play an important role in the life of our Muslim community and may be requested by members of the community for the purpose of Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The issues raised to the Fatwa Committee today are increasingly complex, demanding detailed research and consultations to ensure that the opinions issued by the Committee are rigorous and sound.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The amendments will allow the Committee to tap on a wider range of expertise within the asatizah fraternity to facilitate deliberations.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Assoc Prof Razwana asked how MUIS selects the Fatwa Committee members, so did Mr Faisal Manap.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Can someone apply to be a Fatwa Committee member?

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: MUIS undertakes careful consideration in assessing an individual's capability and expertise and appoint them to the Fatwa Committee.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Since 1990, the Committee has appointed local religious scholars as associate members, thereby enhancing the depth of discussions and providing a training platform for those who may potentially serve as Committee members in the future.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, there is already a process to induct new, even young azatisahs, to get them to understand the fatwa process and, over time, when they qualify and have depth and a grasp of the religion to apply in context, they can be appointed to the Committee.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: While the Fatwa Committee seeks to address issues in a prompt and timely manner, the time taken for an opinion to be issued may vary, depending on the complexity of the issue.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This ensures that the Committee's resources will be focused on matters that require its attention and, in the long term, ensure that requests can be met in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, we have to clear the backlog first and to reduce the number of frivolous fatwas that have been asked all this time.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Should there be complex or urgent matters to be addressed, the Committee will convene meetings more frequently to deliberate on the issues.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: It may not warrant a fatwa, particularly when comprehensive guidance already exists in established sources, such as the religious guidance, or irsyad, issued previously by the Office of the Mufti.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Members have also supported the establishment of a framework to recognise FHCBs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is a positive development, given that Singapore relies heavily on imported food products, some of which would bear the marks of these FHCBs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To Mr Mohamed Sharael Taha, Mr Louis Ng, Dr Syed Harun's questions and to Mr Faisal Manap's questions, too, MUIS' recognition of FHCBs will help our halal-certified food establishments identify halal products from overseas and strengthen their halal regime.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This ensures that all food products used in such establishments, including those that are imported, meet MUIS' halal certification standards.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, MUIS already has these standards and they have to meet those standards.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This includes assessing whether the FHCBs are certifying meat or poultry products from source countries approved or accredited by the Singapore Food Agency and the FHCBs are adopting ISO principles or equivalent standards in their halal certification management systems.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: First, FHCBs will have to undergo mandatory training and assessment to ensure that they are able to comply with Singapore's halal standards and requirements.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: To clarify Dr Syed Harun's query, the amendment is limited to the misuse of halal certificates and marks of MUIS-recognised FHCBs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This will help serve as an added incentive for FHCBs to seek MUIS' recognition.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: We will work with MUIS and industry partners to study the Member's suggestion on how we can further protect our Muslim consumers against the misuse of FHCB marks and certificates.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: MUIS will also charge a fee to FHCBs seeking MUIS' recognition, so as to defray the costs of administering this scheme, such as audit inspections.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: This is similar to MUIS' halal certification for local establishments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The frequency of such audits will be based on MUIS' current risk assessment framework, with a focus on meat and poultry establishments.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I agree with Assoc Prof Razwana Begum on the importance of educating consumers so that they can make informed choices on halal products.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Currently, the public can refer to MUIS' website on the list of recognised FHCBs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: MUIS will continue to provide consumers with relevant information through various channels and explore more ways to make them more accessible.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Overall, this FHCB recognition scheme will help to provide Muslim businesses particularly and consumers generally with greater assurance when purchasing halal products.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I therefore appreciate the feedback shared by Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Assoc Prof Razwana Begum on whether the introduction of Digital Certificates of Marriage would affect the institution of Muslim marriage and measures to prevent errors and scams.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I think Members know that today, when people are getting married, the Kadi or Naib Kadi would call them up first and meet them physically, give them advice before the solemnisation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: So, there is already a process that we have put in place despite all the digitalisation of booking and certification that we have in this amendment.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Therefore, the AMLA ensures that our Muslim community can deal with relevant personal matters, such as marriage, under Muslim law.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Any amendments to the AMLA that involve Muslim law must draw on the advice of the Office of the Mufti, ensuring that all requirements under Muslim law are met before any changes are proposed.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There will continue to be a formal religious marriage ceremony.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Couples will still need to meet the requirements of a valid Muslim marriage as determined by their marriage solemniser, also known as a Kadi or Naib Kadi.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The first instance when they meet, assessment is already being made.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The Kadi or Naib Kadi will assess if all the conditions necessary for a valid solemnisation and registration of a Muslim marriage have been met, in accordance with Muslim law and the provisions of the AMLA.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Prior to the solemnisation, as mentioned just now, the Kadi or Naib Kadi will actually conduct face-to-face sessions with the couple to provide guidance as well as referrals to other relevant support.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: There are cybersecurity safeguards for the digital Certificate of Marriage.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: As with other Government agency websites and accounts, citizens can log in to view their Muslim marriage application or documents via Singpass, which has its own security safeguards.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: The QR code on the digital Certificate will also make it more convenient for parties to verify the authenticity of the document.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: Even as we implement the digital Certificate, the ROMM will provide a hard copy Ceremonial Certificate of Marriage for couples who wish to have it as a keepsake.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M
text: I think it is important to do so.
